title: 8 · Limitations
text:
Choice of library
The same pipeline is applied to leaf area index (LAI), which rises and then falls during the season, by changing var = "lai". Least squares is used for all libraries here.

RPython



trl <- make_trajectories(traj, drv, var = "lai")
P_poly <- cached("cv_lai_poly.rds", cross_validate(Theta, trl, fit_ols))



trl = make_trajectories(traj, drv, var="lai")
P_poly = cross_validate(Theta, trl, fit_ols)



As an alternative library, a B-spline basis in thermal time with the other three drivers entering linearly (splines::bs in R, scipy.interpolate.BSpline in Python; the two bases span the same functions and give the same fit):

RPython



B <- bs(as.vector(drv$U[, , "TT"]), df = 6)
others <- matrix(drv$U[, , -1], ncol = 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("DL", "RAW", "RAD")))
Theta_spl <- array(cbind(B, others), c(dim(drv$U)[1:2], 9),
                   dimnames = list(NULL, NULL, c(paste0("B", 1:6), colnames(others))))
P_spl <- cached("cv_lai_spline.rds", cross_validate(Theta_spl, trl, fit_ols))

base <- lookup_trajectory(trl)
round(rbind(`cubic polynomial` = evaluate(P_poly, trl),
            `B-spline in TT` = evaluate(P_spl, trl),
            baseline = evaluate(base, trl)), 3)



from scipy.interpolate import BSpline

tt = drv.U[:, :, 0].ravel()
inner = np.quantile(tt, [0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
knots = np.r_[[tt.min()] * 4, inner, [tt.max()] * 4]
B = BSpline.design_matrix(tt, knots, 3).toarray()[:, 1:]   # 6 basis functions
others = drv.U[:, :, 1:].reshape(-1, 3)                    # DL, RAW, RAD
terms = [f"B{i}" for i in range(1, 7)] + ["DL", "RAW", "RAD"]
Theta_spl = SimpleNamespace(array=np.column_stack([B, others]).reshape(
    *drv.U.shape[:2], 9), terms=terms)
P_spl = cross_validate(Theta_spl, trl, fit_ols)

base = lookup_trajectory(trl)
print(pd.DataFrame({"cubic polynomial": evaluate(P_poly, trl),
                    "B-spline in TT": evaluate(P_spl, trl),
                    "baseline": evaluate(base, trl)}).T.round(3))





                 trajectory_rmse fixed_day_rmse maturity_rmse
cubic polynomial           0.925          1.272         1.039
B-spline in TT             0.532          0.664         0.562
baseline                   0.473          0.687         0.637

days <- 2:dim(trl$Y)[3] + trl$das0 - 1

  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +

  labs(x = "days after sowing", y = "held-out LAI RMSE") +
  theme_dgxe() +

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
for P, name, colour in [(P_poly, "cubic polynomial", BURGUNDY),
                        (P_spl, "B-spline in TT", BLUE),
                        (base, "baseline", "#9CA3AF")]:
    ax.plot(days, rmse_by_day(P, trl), color=colour, label=name)

A cubic polynomial in the standardised drivers cannot represent the rise and fall of LAI, and its error is larger than that of the baseline throughout. The spline library is considerably better. When the model is inaccurate, the library should be examined before the fitting method.

title: 8 · Limitations
text:
Collinear drivers
Thermal time and day length have a correlation of 0.97. Fitting the same model to the odd and to the even seasons of one genotype gives different coefficients but similar growth rates.

RPython



d <- make_design(Theta, tr, "g114")
odd <- fit_ols(d$X[d$season %% 2 == 1, ], d$dy[d$season %% 2 == 1])
even <- fit_ols(d$X[d$season %% 2 == 0, ], d$dy[d$season %% 2 == 0])
round(rbind(odd, even)[, c("TT", "TT^2", "DL", "DL^2")], 3)

rate <- cbind(1, d$X) %*% cbind(odd, even)      # growth rate on all days
c(correlation = cor(rate[, 1], rate[, 2]),
  max_difference = max(abs(rate[, 1] - rate[, 2])))



d = make_design(Theta, tr, "g114")
odd = d.season % 2 == 0                      # seasons 1, 3, 5, ... (0-based)
b_odd = fit_ols(d.X[odd], d.dy[odd])
b_even = fit_ols(d.X[~odd], d.dy[~odd])
cols = [d.terms.index(t) + 1 for t in ["TT", "TT^2", "DL", "DL^2"]]
print(pd.DataFrame([b_odd[cols], b_even[cols]], index=["odd", "even"],
                   columns=["TT", "TT^2", "DL", "DL^2"]).round(3))

rate = d.X @ np.c_[b_odd[1:], b_even[1:]] + np.r_[b_odd[0], b_even[0]]
print({"correlation": np.corrcoef(rate.T)[0, 1],
       "max_difference": np.abs(rate[:, 0] - rate[:, 1]).max()})





         TT   TT^2    DL   DL^2
odd  -0.067 -0.037 0.039 -0.065
even -0.025 -0.033 0.006 -0.055


   correlation max_difference 
    0.98748717     0.03865562 


The data determine the combined effect of correlated drivers better than each coefficient, so response curves are preferable to individual coefficients for interpretation.

title: 8 · Limitations
text:
Accumulation of error
The regression is performed on daily increments, whereas the prediction is their cumulative sum. A small bias in the daily increment therefore accumulates.

RPython



P <- cached("cv_stlsq.rds", cross_validate(Theta, tr, fit_stlsq))
step_error <- P[, , -1] - P[, , -dim(P)[3]]           # predicted increments
step_error <- step_error - (tr$Y[, , -1] - tr$Y[, , -dim(tr$Y)[3]])
c(daily_increment_rmse = sqrt(mean(step_error^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
  trajectory_rmse = evaluate(P, tr)[[1]])



P = cross_validate(Theta, tr, fit_stlsq)
step_error = np.diff(P, axis=2) - np.diff(tr.Y, axis=2)
print({"daily_increment_rmse": np.sqrt(np.nanmean(step_error ** 2)),
       "trajectory_rmse": evaluate(P, tr)["trajectory_rmse"]})





daily_increment_rmse      trajectory_rmse 
          0.02794568           0.52631617 


For this reason the model is assessed on the simulated trajectory and not on the daily increments.

title: 6 · Interpretation
text:
Effect of a single driver
The effect of one driver cannot be read by varying it alone while the others are held fixed, since the drivers are correlated in real weather:

RPython



Z <- as.data.frame(observed_points(drv, tr))       # standardised drivers
round(cor(Z), 2)



Z = observed_points(drv, tr)                       # standardised drivers
print(Z.corr().round(2))





       TT    DL   RAW   RAD
TT   1.00  0.97 -0.65  0.72
DL   0.97  1.00 -0.67  0.74
RAW -0.65 -0.67  1.00 -0.58
RAD  0.72  0.74 -0.58  1.00


Accumulated local effects (ALE) vary the driver only within narrow intervals around values that occur, using the observed values of the other drivers, and accumulate the resulting changes in the growth rate. The iml package computes them for any model that provides a prediction function; here the model is the growth rate of a genotype.

RPython



predictor <- function(coef, pairs = FALSE) {
  rate <- function(model, newdata) {
    L <- library_matrix(as.matrix(newdata), pairs = pairs)
    as.vector(cbind(1, L) %*% model)
  }
  Predictor$new(coef, data = Z, predict.function = rate)
}

natural <- function(z, j) z * drv$scale[j] + drv$center[j]     # original units
ale_genotype <- function(g, j) {
  effect <- FeatureEffect$new(predictor(coefs[, g]), drv$drivers[j],
                              method = "ale", grid.size = 24)$results
  data.frame(genotype = g, driver = factor(drv$drivers[j], drv$drivers),
             x = natural(effect[[drv$drivers[j]]], j), effect = effect$.value)
}
cells <- expand.grid(g = tr$genotypes, j = seq_along(drv$drivers),
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
curves <- cached("ale_genotypes.rds", do.call(rbind, Map(ale_genotype, cells$g, cells$j)))

title: 6 · Interpretation
text:
Interactions and partial dependence
The 12-term library is additive in the drivers: the effect of one driver does not depend on the others, and ALE and partial dependence coincide. With products of drivers (36 terms, backward elimination to 20 terms) they differ. For g114, partial dependence averages the growth rate over all observed days while one driver is set to each value in turn.

RPython



Theta2 <- make_library(drv, pairs = TRUE)
d2 <- make_design(Theta2, tr, "g114")
pred2 <- predictor(fit_subset(d2$X, d2$dy, k = 20, method = "backward"), TRUE)

effects <- function(j) {
  feature <- drv$drivers[j]
  ale <- FeatureEffect$new(pred2, feature, "ale", grid.size = 24)$results
  pdp <- FeatureEffect$new(pred2, feature, "pdp", grid.size = 24)$results
  pdp$x <- natural(pdp[[feature]], j)
  pdp$driver <- factor(feature, drv$drivers)
  pdp$.value <- pdp$.value - mean(pdp$.value)
  ale$x <- natural(ale[[feature]], j)
  ale$driver <- pdp$driver[1]
  pdp[[feature]] <- NULL
  ale[[feature]] <- NULL
  list(pdp = pdp, ale = ale)
}
parts <- lapply(1:2, effects)



Theta2 = make_library(drv, pairs=True)
d2 = make_design(Theta2, tr, "g114")
rate2 = GrowthRate(fit_subset(d2.X, d2.dy, k=20, method="backward"), pairs=True)

def effects(feature):
    j = drv.drivers.index(feature)
    a = ale(Z, rate2, [feature], grid_size=24, include_CI=False, plot=False)
    grid = np.linspace(Z[feature].min(), Z[feature].max(), 24)
    pdp = np.array([rate2.predict(Z.assign(**{feature: v})).mean()
                    for v in grid])
    return (natural(grid, j), pdp - pdp.mean(),

title: 4 · Fitting
text: Every method maps the design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) and the increments \(\Delta\mathbf{y}\) of one genotype to a coefficient vector, with the intercept first. A method is therefore a function fit(X, dy), and methods can be exchanged freely. Genotype g001 is used here.

title: 4 · Fitting
4 · Fitting
text:
Subset selection and thresholding
Best-subset selection and backward elimination keep \(k\) terms (leaps; in Python the residual sums of squares are computed directly from the Gram matrix). Sequential thresholded least squares (STLSQ) is the algorithm of the original SINDy method: fit, remove the terms whose scaled coefficient is below a threshold, and refit on the remaining terms.

RPython


## Best subset (exhaustive) or backward elimination with k terms, by leaps.
fit_subset <- function(X, dy, k = 8, method = "exhaustive") {
  b <- coef(leaps::regsubsets(X, dy, nvmax = k, method = method), k)
  full <- setNames(numeric(ncol(X) + 1), c("1", colnames(X)))
  full[c("1", names(b)[-1])] <- b
  full
}

## Sequential thresholded least squares (the original SINDy algorithm): refit
## on the active terms and remove those whose scaled coefficient is below the
## threshold, until no term is removed.
fit_stlsq <- function(X, dy, threshold = 0.05) {
  size <- apply(X, 2, sd) / sd(dy)         # puts all coefficients on one scale
  active <- colnames(X)
  repeat {
    b <- lm.fit(cbind(`1` = 1, X[, active, drop = FALSE]), dy)$coefficients
    keep <- abs(b[active]) * size[active] >= threshold
    if (all(keep) || !any(keep)) break
    active <- active[keep]
  }
  full <- setNames(numeric(ncol(X) + 1), c("1", colnames(X)))
  full[names(b)] <- b
  full
}


# Best subset (exhaustive) or backward elimination with k terms. Everything is
# computed from the centred Gram matrix G and c = X'dy: a subset S has
# residual sum of squares dy'dy - c_S' G_SS^-1 c_S, and removing term j from S
# increases it by b_j^2 / (G_SS^-1)_jj.
def fit_subset(X, dy, k=8, method="exhaustive"):
    Xc, yc = X - X.mean(axis=0), dy - dy.mean()
    G, c = Xc.T @ Xc, Xc.T @ yc
    if method == "exhaustive":
        subsets = np.array(list(combinations(range(X.shape[1]), k)))
        blocks = G[subsets[:, :, None], subsets[:, None, :]]
        b = np.linalg.solve(blocks, c[subsets][..., None])[..., 0]
        keep = subsets[np.argmax((b * c[subsets]).sum(axis=1))]
    else:
        keep = np.arange(X.shape[1])
        while len(keep) > k:
            inv = np.linalg.inv(G[np.ix_(keep, keep)])
            increase = (inv @ c[keep]) ** 2 / np.diag(inv)
            keep = np.delete(keep, np.argmin(increase))
    b = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    b[keep] = np.linalg.solve(G[np.ix_(keep, keep)], c[keep])
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - X.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])


# Sequential thresholded least squares (the original SINDy algorithm): refit
# on the active terms and remove those whose scaled coefficient is below the
# threshold, until no term is removed.
def fit_stlsq(X, dy, threshold=0.05):
    size = X.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / dy.std(ddof=1)    # common scale
    active = np.arange(X.shape[1])
    while True:
        b = fit_ols(X[:, active], dy)
        keep = np.abs(b[1:]) * size[active] >= threshold
        if keep.all() or not keep.any():
            break
        active = active[keep]
    full = np.zeros(X.shape[1] + 1)
    full[0], full[1 + active] = b[0], b[1:]
    return full

title: Sparse identification of crop growth dynamics

This workshop fits a daily growth equation for wheat biomass to simulated field-trial data in R. The growth rate is written as a sparse combination of candidate functions of the environment (SINDy), the coefficients are obtained by regression, and the equation is validated on seasons that were not used for fitting.

title: 1 · Method
text: Schematic. Environmental drivers \(U\) and the response \(Y\) are measured over time. The growth rate of \(Y\) is regressed on a library \(\Theta(Y, U)\) of candidate functions; a sparse coefficient matrix \(\Xi\) selects the terms of the equation.

title: 1 · Method
text: Schematic. Environmental drivers \(U\) and the response \(Y\) are measured over time. The growth rate of \(Y\) is regressed on a library \(\Theta(Y, U)\) of candidate functions; a sparse coefficient matrix \(\Xi\) selects the terms of the equation.

title: 1 · Method
1 · Method
text:
Regression
Let \(y_i = y(t_i)\) be observations on consecutive days. The increments \(\Delta y_i = y_{i+1} - y_i\) approximate \(\dot{y}(t_i)\) for a time step of one day.



Observed biomass of one genotype in one season (a), and its daily increments (b). The regression is performed on the increments.


Collecting the increments in a vector \(\Delta\mathbf{y}\) and the library values in a matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) with entries \(X_{ij} = \theta_j(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{u}_i)\) gives
\[
\Delta\mathbf{y} \approx \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
The coefficients enter linearly, so they can be estimated by regression, for example by least squares
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \Delta\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 .
\]
Any regression method can be used. Step 4 compares several.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Sparsity
A short equation is easier to interpret and less prone to overfitting than one with many terms. Sparsity is obtained by regression methods that set coefficients to zero: thresholding of small coefficients (sequential thresholded least squares, the original SINDy algorithm), an \(\ell_1\) penalty (lasso), or subset selection. The number of retained terms balances accuracy and complexity and is chosen by validation.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Solution
Given \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\) and the drivers, the equation is solved forward in time from an initial value \(y_0\) with the same one-day step,
\[
y_{i+1} = y_i + \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{u}_i)^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} .
\]
If the library depends on the drivers only, this is a cumulative sum, \(y_i = y_0 + \sum_{s<i} \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{u}_s)^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\), and no ODE solver is needed.



Season 1998 of one genotype, predicted by a model fitted to the other seasons. The predicted daily growth (a) is accumulated from the initial value \(y_0\) (b) and compared with the APSIM trajectory.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Genotypes
Each genotype \(g\) has its own coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_g\), estimated from the trajectories of that genotype in all available seasons.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Validation
The independent units are seasons, since the weather of neighbouring days is strongly correlated. The model of a genotype is validated by leave-one-season-out cross-validation: each season is predicted from a model fitted to the other seasons and compared with the observed trajectory.



Leave-one-season-out cross-validation. Each row is one fit; the season in red is left out and predicted.

Drivers
The drivers \(u_1, \dots, u_4\) (TT, DL, RAW, RAD) are standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The response does not enter this step.

RPython


make_drivers <- function(wx, drivers = c("TT", "DL", "RAW", "RAD")) {
  years <- sort(unique(wx$year))
  das0 <- min(wx$das)
  nd <- max(wx$das) - das0 + 1
  U <- array(NA_real_, c(length(years), nd, length(drivers)),
             dimnames = list(years, NULL, drivers))
  for (j in seq_along(drivers)) {
    i <- cbind(match(wx$year, years), wx$das - das0 + 1, j)
    U[i] <- wx[[drivers[j]]]
  }
  # seasons end on different days: pad with the last value (never fitted)
  for (y in seq_along(years)) {
    for (j in seq_along(drivers)) {
      u <- U[y, , j]
      U[y, is.na(u), j] <- tail(u[!is.na(u)], 1)
    }
  }
  center <- apply(U, 3, mean)
  scale <- apply(U, 3, function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))
  list(U = sweep(sweep(U, 3, center), 3, scale, "/"), years = years,
       das0 = das0, drivers = drivers, center = center, scale = scale)
}


def make_drivers(wx, drivers=DRIVERS):
    years = np.sort(wx["year"].unique())
    das0 = wx["das"].min()
    U = np.full((len(years), wx["das"].max() - das0 + 1, len(drivers)), np.nan)
    y = np.searchsorted(years, wx["year"])
    U[y, (wx["das"] - das0).to_numpy(), :] = wx[drivers].to_numpy()
    for s in range(len(years)):                  # seasons end on different days
        for j in range(len(drivers)):            # pad with the last value
            u = U[s, :, j]
            u[np.isnan(u)] = u[~np.isnan(u)][-1]
    center = U.mean(axis=(0, 1))
    scale = U.std(axis=(0, 1))
    return SimpleNamespace(U=(U - center) / scale, years=years, das0=das0,
                           drivers=list(drivers), center=center, scale=scale)

## nend[g, y] is the number of daily steps of trajectory (g, y).
make_trajectories <- function(traj, drv, var = "biomass") {
  gen <- sort(unique(traj$genotype))
  Y <- array(NA_real_, c(length(gen), length(drv$years), dim(drv$U)[2]),
             dimnames = list(gen, drv$years, NULL))
  i <- cbind(match(traj$genotype, gen), match(traj$year, drv$years),
             traj$das - drv$das0 + 1)
  Y[i] <- traj[[var]]
  nend <- apply(Y, c(1, 2), function(v) sum(!is.na(v)) - 1)
  list(Y = Y, nend = nend, genotypes = gen, years = drv$years,
       das0 = drv$das0)
}


# nend[g, s] is the number of daily steps of trajectory (g, s).
def make_trajectories(traj, drv, var="biomass"):
    genotypes = np.sort(traj["genotype"].unique())
    Y = np.full((len(genotypes), len(drv.years), drv.U.shape[1]), np.nan)
    g = np.searchsorted(genotypes, traj["genotype"])
    s = np.searchsorted(drv.years, traj["year"])
    Y[g, s, traj["das"] - drv.das0] = traj[var]
    return SimpleNamespace(Y=Y, nend=(~np.isnan(Y)).sum(axis=2) - 1,
                           genotypes=genotypes, years=drv.years,
                           das0=drv.das0)

## Rows: all days of all seasons. X: library at day t. dy: y(t + 1) - y(t).
make_design <- function(Theta, tr, genotype) {
  g <- match(genotype, tr$genotypes)
  n <- tr$nend[g, ]
  seasons <- seq_along(tr$years)
  X <- lapply(seasons, function(y) matrix(Theta[y, 1:n[y], ], n[y]))

  colnames(X) <- dimnames(Theta)[[3]]
  list(X = X, dy = unlist(dy), season = rep(seasons, n))

# Rows: all days of all seasons. X: library at day t. dy: y(t + 1) - y(t).
def make_design(Theta, tr, genotype):

    dy = np.concatenate([np.diff(tr.Y[g, s, :n[s] + 1]) for s in seasons])
    season = np.repeat(np.arange(len(tr.years)), n)
    return SimpleNamespace(X=X, dy=dy, season=season, terms=Theta.terms)

5 · Validation
text:
Leave-one-season-out cross-validation
For every genotype and every season, the model is fitted to the other 30 seasons of that genotype and used to predict the left-out season from its drivers, starting from the mean initial biomass of the training seasons.

RPython


## Each season is predicted by a model fitted to the other seasons of the same
## genotype, starting from the mean initial biomass of those seasons.
## Returns P[genotype, season, day].
cross_validate <- function(Theta, tr, fit, genotypes = tr$genotypes) {
  P <- array(NA_real_, dim(tr$Y))
  for (g in match(genotypes, tr$genotypes)) {
    d <- make_design(Theta, tr, tr$genotypes[g])
    for (v in seq_along(tr$years)) {
      train <- d$season != v
      coef <- fit(d$X[train, ], d$dy[train])
      P[g, v, ] <- simulate(coef, Theta[v, , ], mean(tr$Y[g, -v, 1]))
    }
  }
  P
}

## RMSE over whole trajectories, on a fixed day (array index; 99 is day 113
## after sowing) and at maturity. Genotypes that were not predicted are ignored.
evaluate <- function(P, tr, fixed_day = 99) {
  err <- P - tr$Y
  err[, , 1] <- NA                                # the initial value is given
  last <- cbind(as.vector(row(tr$nend)), as.vector(col(tr$nend)),
                as.vector(tr$nend) + 1)
  rmse <- function(e) sqrt(mean(e^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  c(trajectory_rmse = rmse(err), fixed_day_rmse = rmse(err[, , fixed_day]),
    maturity_rmse = rmse(err[last]))
}


# Each season is predicted by a model fitted to the other seasons of the same
# genotype, starting from the mean initial biomass of those seasons.
# Returns P[genotype, season, day].
def cross_validate(Theta, tr, fit, genotypes=None):
    P = np.full(tr.Y.shape, np.nan)
    for g in (tr.genotypes if genotypes is None else genotypes):
        i = list(tr.genotypes).index(g)
        d = make_design(Theta, tr, g)
        for s in range(len(tr.years)):
            train = d.season != s
            coef = fit(d.X[train], d.dy[train])
            y0 = np.delete(tr.Y[i, :, 0], s).mean()
            P[i, s] = simulate(coef, Theta.array[s], y0)
    return P


# RMSE over whole trajectories, on a fixed day (days after sowing) and at
# maturity. Genotypes that were not predicted are ignored.
def evaluate(P, tr, fixed_day=113):
    err = P - tr.Y
    err[:, :, 0] = np.nan                        # the initial value is given
    g, s = np.indices(tr.nend.shape)

    def rmse(e):
        return np.sqrt(np.nanmean(e ** 2))

    return {"trajectory_rmse": rmse(err),
            "fixed_day_rmse": rmse(err[:, :, fixed_day - tr.das0]),
            "maturity_rmse": rmse(err[g, s, tr.nend])}

## Baseline without weather: each trajectory is the mean curve of the same
## genotype in the other seasons (held at its last value once all other
## seasons have ended), with the true initial value.
lookup_trajectory <- function(tr) {
  hold_last <- function(v) replace(v, is.nan(v), tail(v[!is.nan(v)], 1))
  P <- array(NA_real_, dim(tr$Y))
  for (y in seq_along(tr$years)) {
    m <- apply(tr$Y[, -y, , drop = FALSE], c(1, 3), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
    P[, y, ] <- t(apply(m, 1, hold_last))
    P[, y, 1] <- tr$Y[, y, 1]
  }
  P
}


# Baseline without weather: each trajectory is the mean curve of the same
# genotype in the other seasons (held at its last value once all other
# seasons have ended), with the true initial value.
def lookup_trajectory(tr):
    seen = ~np.isnan(tr.Y)
    total, count = np.nansum(tr.Y, axis=1), seen.sum(axis=1)  # genotype x day
    n = count[:, None, :] - seen                              # other seasons
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        P = (total[:, None, :] - np.nan_to_num(tr.Y)) / n
    last = (n > 0).sum(axis=2, keepdims=True) - 1             # last day seen
    P = np.where(n > 0, P, np.take_along_axis(P, last, axis=2))
    P[:, :, 0] = tr.Y[:, :, 0]
    return P

## Pd, Yd: genotype x season matrices of predicted and APSIM biomass on one
## day. For each season: Spearman correlation of the two rankings and overlap
## of the predicted and true top 10 %.
rank_scores <- function(Pd, Yd, top = 0.1) {
  k <- max(1, round(top * nrow(Yd)))
  score <- function(y) {
    overlap <- intersect(order(-Pd[, y])[1:k], order(-Yd[, y])[1:k])
    data.frame(year = y, rho = cor(Pd[, y], Yd[, y], method = "spearman"),
               top = length(overlap) / k)
  }
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(ncol(Yd)), score))
}


# Pd, Yd: genotype x season matrices of predicted and APSIM biomass on one
# day. For each season: Spearman correlation of the two rankings and overlap
# of the predicted and true top 10 %.
def rank_scores(Pd, Yd, top=0.1):
    from scipy.stats import spearmanr
    k = max(1, round(top * Yd.shape[0]))
    rho, overlap = [], []
    for s in range(Yd.shape[1]):
        rho.append(spearmanr(Pd[:, s], Yd[:, s])[0])
        best = set(np.argsort(-Pd[:, s])[:k]) & set(np.argsort(-Yd[:, s])[:k])
        overlap.append(len(best) / k)
    return np.array(rho), np.array(overlap)

title: 9 · Extensions
text:
Coupled states
In steps 4 to 8 the library depends on the drivers only, so the solution is a cumulative sum. In a crop, a larger leaf area intercepts more light and increases biomass growth. Including the state in the library gives a coupled system in the leaf area index \(L\) and the biomass \(B\), with \(\mathbf{y} = (L, B)\):
\[
\dot{L} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_L(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u})^\top \boldsymbol{\xi}_L, \qquad
\dot{B} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_B(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u})^\top \boldsymbol{\xi}_B .
\]
The regression is unchanged, with the observed states in the library. The solution requires numerical integration, and errors in the states feed back into the rates.



Fitting and prediction for three model variants: weather only (driving-only), coupled with leaf area index \(L\) predicted by its own equation, and driven by measured \(L\).

title: 9 · Extensions
text:
Physical terms in the library
A candidate term for biomass growth is the light intercepted by the canopy, \(I = 1 - \exp(-0.5\,L)\), multiplied by radiation: \(\mathrm{d}B/\mathrm{d}t \ni I \cdot \mathrm{RAD}\).

Further directions

Other regression methods: any method with the signature fit(X, dy). Bayesian regression with sparsity-inducing priors provides uncertainty for the coefficients at higher computational cost.
Several sites and joint fitting of genotypes: coefficients shared between genotypes, with genotype-specific deviations, use the data of all genotypes for each equation. Pooling sites adds variation in the weather.
New genotypes: prediction for a genotype not used in fitting requires additional information about it, for example its parameter values. This is not treated here.
Other responses: step 8 shows leaf area index as an example.
